e-Cigarettes

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
how safe are e-cigarettes?

Unique Selling Point:
Are so-called Reduced Risk Products really that much safer than smoking cigarettes? We ask the World Health Organization for the facts.

Summary:
Ever since tough anti-tobacco legislation banned smoking in public places, South African nicotine addicts have had the option of puffing on e-cigarettes. It's accepted that these are not dangerous to the puffers or the people around them. But is this really the case? Should we be concerned if our colleagues and friends are vaping in the same room?

Further information:
Do Reduced Risk Products pose a threat to your health? We hear from Philip Morris tobacco company how their new heated tobacco products have removed 90% of the harmful chemicals from smoking. But is this enough?
DO these products actually help people stop smoking, or do they simply make them feel good about their addiction? And what does South African legislation say about these products?

Press Release:


E-cigarettes
Are e-cigarettes really that much safer than ordinary cigarettes? Tobacco companies claim that through their new
heated tobacco products they have removed 90% of the chemicals harmful to smokers. Carte Blanche visits to the
World Health Organisation in Switzerland to get some answers.

Script:


E-CIGARETTES

V/O: In 1604 King James I of England described smoking as “a custom loathsome to the eye, hateful to the nose, harmful to the brain and dangerous to the lungs.” It would take another 400 years before modern science concurred with His Majesty, and global public sentiment turned against tobacco.

Link: This is the Executive Boardroom of the World Health Organization, and it’s here that global health issues are discussed amongst member states – very often the question of tobacco control.

Dr Prasad: WHO’s position has been that all forms of tobacco are harmful and it kills. Now we have more than 7 million tobacco-attributable deaths in the world.

V/O: Dr Vinay Prasad heads up the Tobacco Free Initiative for the WHO in Geneva, and advises governments on tobacco control.

Dr Prasad: The Framework Convention now has 180 parties, and all of them have committed to reducing tobacco-use globally. Now the target is to reduce tobacco-use by 30% relative reduction by 2030.

V/O: South Africa was one of the first countries to implement tough anti-smoking legislation in 2001, which restricted smoking to designated areas only, and banned cigarette advertising. But a few years later came the invention of the e-cigarette, widely seen as a smoke-free, safer alternative. These work by heating a liquid that usually contains nicotine, to generate an aerosol or vapour that the user inhales.

Tony: I vape a lot, I’ve always got this with me.

V/O: Tony Maher smoked 30 cigarettes a day for 30 years, before switching to electronic cigarettes 3 years ago.

Tony: I don’t feel like I’ve given up, I just feel like I’ve changed my method of ingestion.

Derek: Tony don’t you feel that this is just as addictive as tobacco?

Tony: Well it’s nicotine, so I think it’s the same addiction and I am a nicotine addict, I know that.

Derek: So, what would you say is different about your health now?

Tony: Well I breathe clearly and freely, I’m not coughing, I don’t have the same problems with tasting, so it has improved my health a lot. 

V/O: But does this mean that Electronic Nicotine Delivery Systems or ENDS, are risk-free?

Dr Prasad: It's still not established as to the extent of harm from ENDS. It's not a safe product, the risks exist in terms of direct exposure - so there are carcinogens which exist in ENDS. But for those who are already addicted to tobacco use – if they want to move over to ENDS – hundred percent. But the first recommendation from WHO is don’t use any form of tobacco, including ENDS.

V/O: But according to the United States Surgeon General, the use of e-cigarettes by high school students has tripled in the last 5 years.

Sfx: “Some say e-cigarettes aren’t dangerous. But science shows nicotine can harm teens developing brains, no matter how they’re exposed. Let’s do an experiment to find out. Here’s a teen who won’t be using e-cigarettes. Now we one willing to risk their brain development. Care to volunteer your kid?”

Muazzam: I’ve been smoking, vaping, for two years now. In school, I feel that I can run better, I have more energy, I have way more breath than before.

Derek: So look at your class. How many guys in the class?

Muazzam: About forty of us.

Derek: Forty – how many vape?

Muazzam; I would say half of it.

Peter: We know that in South Africa the target market is the youth because they’re flavoured - all sorts of romantic, exotic flavours -and it’s appealing to the youth. And they are promoted as being safer than regular cigarettes. Well they might be a little safer – we think – but they are not safe. They certainly are not harmless.

V/O: Peter Ucko heads up TAG, the Tobacco, Alcohol and Gambling Advisory, Advocacy and Action Group.

Peter: The youth is the growing market, and the danger is that will lead to smoking regular combustible cigarettes.

Derek: To what extent have e-cigarettes become part of big tobacco?

Prasad: In the last couple of years all the big tobacco has acquired the smaller ENDS companies, and all of them now have their product.

Sfx: “Come to where the flavor is. Come to Marlboro country.”

V/O: We went to Lausanne in Switzerland to speak to big tobacco. Philip Morris International makes the world’s top selling cigarette - Marlboro. But they claim they want their customers to quit cigarettes.

Tommaso: Our aim as a company is that one day all smokers switch to smoke-free products; products that do not combust and have the potential to be much less harmful alternatives than cigarettes.

V/O: Global Director of Communications, Tommaso di Giovanni, believes they are meeting customer’s needs.

Tommaso: Smokers are concerned about the health effects of smoking, and look for reduced risk products. That's exactly why we believe that addressing that demand makes business sense. We have invested over $3 billion in the last 8 or 9 years. We have 430 researchers.

V/O: Their latest heat-not-burn device heats tobacco at temperatures below combustion, and it is this that eliminates over a hundred harmful chemical substances according to Director for Scientific Engagement, Dr Ruth Dempsey.

Ruth: Those 100 chemical substances are produced during the combustion processes. If you eliminate that combustion you will significantly reduce or eliminate those harmful components. The data that we have so far shows that around about 90 to 95% reduction in those harmful constituents within smoke.

Derek: Do you share this research with the WHO?

Ruth: Oh, we’d love to – we would very happily talk to them about our research.

Derek: So why don’t you speak to them?

Ruth: As far as I’m aware it’s the WHO who are reluctant to talk to us.

Derek: Companies like Philip Morris say you don’t even look at their research?

Prasad: We need to go back to history: in the 60's, 70's and the 80's a lot of research was done by the tobacco industry, and all the facts of that research never got out until there was independent research to demonstrate that tobacco kills because of cancers, cardio-vascular diseases, stroke. And we do not trust any industry-led research because for that reason. 

Ruth: I've been working in the tobacco industry for over 30 years, and I've never been asked to lie about the research. All the work I've done has been open and honest, and I think very solid research, and it's been the grounds for where we are now.

Derek: Tommaso what do you see happening in ten years’ time?

Tommaso: I hope that in ten years’ time we will be very advanced towards a smoke-free future, where smokers quit cigarettes and only adopt these new products.

V/O: We asked some users of the heat-not-burn device for feedback:

Kaye: You just keep puffing, but you can taste the nicotine…

V/O: Kaye Barkmann has been smoking 10 cigarettes a day for over 40 years.

Derek: Kaye, Philip Morris say that this is 95% safer than smoking cigarettes. Do you believe that?

Kaye: You know I actually do because you’re not getting that kick at the back of your throat. I think I’d like to believe that.

Prasad: All of this is tobacco industry data. There is not enough evidence of that because the long-term health consequences are difficult to judge. So we will have to wait until independent research is conducted. 

Link: In South Africa, there is no legislation against smoking e-cigarettes or vapes in public places, so you can puff away in offices or restaurants like this. But it seems that’s about to change.

Peter: Proposed amendments to the legislation will include e-cigarettes and other devices under the definition of tobacco products, and be banned the same way that tobacco products are.
